parts: Once, a person connected your phone call by plugging in a cable.
No dial. No computer. Just someone who heard you say a number.
So how did a phone call find its way before computers?
Wikipedia says several places claim the first telephone exchange. The earliest dates are in the late eighteen seventies.
On a vertical panel, each phone line ended in a jack.
According to Wikipedia, in many systems a caller lifted the receiver, and a lamp lit at the operator's position.
Wikipedia's article on telephone exchanges gives the operator's question: number, please?
Then the operator used a pair of plugs joined by cords to link your line with the line you wanted.
One cord answered your call. The other rang the line you wanted.
A call to another town needed a trunk line to another operator.
Wikipedia gives an average of fifteen minutes to complete a long-distance call in nineteen eighteen.
In nineteen forty-three, with military calls getting priority, it says some calls routed through manual trunks could take up to two hours.
Wikipedia adds that operators also handled billing, busy-line checks, and emergency calls.
Here is our reading. The operator was a human router: the number was the address, and the cords were the road.
Then came the automatic exchange.
According to Wikipedia, Almon Strowger, an undertaker, conceived an automatic switch in eighteen eighty-eight and was awarded a patent in eighteen ninety-one.
Wikipedia says he became convinced that operators were deliberately interfering with his calls.
It gives a rival account from a telephone company manager in nineteen thirteen, who blamed a metal sign. So the cause of his trouble is disputed.
The dial sent pulses for each digit. Wikipedia says one set raised a shaft to the right level, and the next set rotated it to the right contact.
Extra stages let the system reach many more customers.
Wikipedia says the Strowger company's first commercial exchange opened in La Porte, Indiana, in eighteen ninety-two, with around seventy-five subscribers.
Wikipedia says automatic dial systems spread partly to reduce labor costs as usage grew.
In our reading, operators faded out slowly. Wikipedia says a hand-crank exchange in Maine was converted in nineteen eighty-three, and some manual switchboards still ran in nineteen ninety-one.
Today, many calls run on digital exchanges. Wikipedia says they sample each voice call eight thousand times per second.
Wikipedia says that in digital telephony, switches handle the data packets in between.
Here is our reading. The job did not vanish. The operator's hand became a program that picks the path.
In our reading, when you dial, or tap a name, a switch somewhere is doing what a hand once did.
Some hidden tricks are not machines at all. Look at a pond on a calm day.
A tiny insect walks on the water. Why does it not sink?
